find: The Hajj commemorates the trials of the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and his family, and the events it re-enacts are rooted in the pre-Islamic history of Mecca.
replace: The Hajj commemorates the trials of the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and his family, and the events it re-enacts took place centuries before the Prophet Muhammad was born.
note: F6: Muslims hold that Ibrahim submitted to the one God, so the Hajj's founding events are not 'pre-Islamic'; that phrase normally names the age of idol worship.

find: On arrival in Mecca, pilgrims enter a state of ritual purity (ihram), wearing two plain white sheets that remove all distinctions of wealth, nationality, and status.
replace: Before they reach Mecca, at boundary points called miqat, pilgrims enter a state of ritual purity (ihram). Men wear two plain white sheets; women wear plain, modest dress. Ihram removes all distinctions of wealth, nationality, and status.
note: F3: ihram is entered at the miqat before Mecca, and the two white sheets are men's dress only.

find: Pilgrims wear identical ihram garments, removing all distinctions of status
replace: Pilgrims wear plain ihram dress, removing all distinctions of status
note: F4: ihram dress is not identical - men wear two white sheets, women plain modest clothing.

expect: Plain white ihram garments, to remove all distinctions of wealth, nationality, and status before Allah.
value: Men wear two plain white sheets and women wear plain modest dress, so that wealth and status are hidden before Allah.
note: F5: same ihram dress error in recall practice.

find: Surah 46, verse 33 and surah 3, verse 16 are among the passages the spec highlights as scriptural anchors for this doctrine.
replace: Two passages are often used to support it. Surah 46, verse 33 teaches that the God who created the heavens and the earth is able to give life to the dead. In surah 3, verse 16 believers pray for forgiveness and for protection from the punishment of the Fire.
note: F1: removes the false claim that these are set references for this paper's akhirah content, and tells students what the verses actually say.

expect: Mastering: Two fully developed beliefs, each linked to a source of authority. E.g. Belief 1: Jannah (paradise) is a place of peace and nearness to God — the Qur'an (3:16) describes God's reward for those who are mindful of Him. Belief 2: Jahannam (hell) is the consequence of rejecting God's guidance — surah 46:33 reminds believers that God who created them has the power to raise the dead. Concludes by connecting akhirah to al-Qadr and human accountability. Secure: Two beliefs explained with at least one source; some development of each. Developing: Two beliefs stated but one or both lack development or source. Emerging: One belief mentioned with little development.
value: Mastering: Two fully developed beliefs, each linked to a source of authority. E.g. Belief 1: Jannah (paradise) is a place of peace and nearness to God — the Qur'an (3:15) describes gardens with rivers flowing beneath them for those who are mindful of God. Belief 2: Jahannam (hell) is the consequence of rejecting God's guidance — surah 46:33 reminds believers that God who created them has the power to raise the dead. Concludes by connecting akhirah to al-Qadr and human accountability. Secure: Two beliefs explained with at least one source; some development of each. Developing: Two beliefs stated but one or both lack development or source. Emerging: One belief mentioned with little development.
note: F2: 3:15 describes the reward; 3:16 is the believers' prayer for forgiveness.
